newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan debt trade may react slowly to incentives.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan debt trade may react slowly to incentives.

text.p: Incentives offered to foreign investors may eventually boost Pakistan's capital market, but analysts said on Wednesday the immediate response might be marginal unless the economy improves.
A government package announced on Tuesday included scrapping taxes payable by foreign investors on earnings from government and private debt instruments.

Foreign institutions and banks previously had to pay up to 60 percent and individuals 32.5 percent in non-refundable withholding tax and an additional 2.5 percent as Zakat (Islamic tax) on earnings from debt instruments.

"Any major investment flow in debt instruments will have to be preceded by concrete improvement in the overall economy and corporate sector earnings," Jahanzeb Naseer, research head at Jardine Fleming Pakistan, told Reuters.
He said foreign investors would remain exposed to currency exchange risk and would have few opportunities for trading because Pakistan's secondary debt market was still illiquid.
The rupee has lost 14.29 percent of its dollar value so far in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June), against 13.2 percent in the whole of 1995/96.
Analysts said foreign banks based in Pakistan were among the major primary market investors, particularly in government debt.

This was mainly because the central bank offered them exchange risk cover, in return for a fee, on foreign currency deposits brought in from abroad. Other foreign investors will not get this facility.

Under the new package, foreign investors, including overseas Pakistanis, will be allowed to invest in bonds and term finance certificates, including three-, five- and 10-year federal investment bonds and six-month short-term federal bonds, listed in Pakistani stock exchanges in the secondary market through special convertible rupee accounts.
"Corporate debt instruments may benefit if they are prepared to raise their yield to the extent where it becomes attractive to foreign investment," Naseer said.
Kaleem Aziz, research head at ING Baring Securities, said that despite the exchange risk, foreign investors stood to get a tax-free yield of seven to eight percent on most debt issues.
"The change is for real in the long term, but foreigners will wait until Pakistan's economic numbers start showing steady improvement," Aziz said.
Naz Chohan, head of the fixed-income department at brokerage house KASB & Co, said high yields on short-term government paper might still attract some foreign investment.

"The yield on local currency six-month debt (is) 17.25 percent...which is extremely attractive, and I think a lot of people are now comfortable with six months to a year risk on Pakistan even if they have to take the foreign currency exposure themselves," Chohan told Reuters Financial Television.

The chief economist at a foreign bank said the government should introduce regulations to avert any damaging fluctuation in the debt market and enable foreign investors to feel comfortable buying rupee-denominated securities.

"The government has to understand that there is a differnce between negotiating a debt agreement with a multilateral donor, where goodwill plays a part, and allowing foreign investors a stake in domestic debt, where market forces rule," he said.
